chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: In April the troops were energized by news of the Emperor's arrival, but Rostov had no chance to attend the review at Bartenstein, as the Pavlograds were stationed at the outposts far from there.

They were bivouacking. Denisov and Rostov were living in an earth dugout that the soldiers had made for them, roofed with branches and turf. The dugout was built in the style that had become fashionable: a trench three and a half feet wide, nearly five feet deep, and eight feet long. At one end, steps were cut into the earth, forming the entrance and vestibule. The trench itself was the room, in which the lucky ones — like the squadron commander — had a plank laid on supports at the far end to serve as a table. On each side, the earth was cut back about two and a half feet, creating beds and couches. The roof was built so you could stand up in the middle and even sit up on the beds if you stayed close to the table. Denisov, who lived well because his soldiers liked him, also had a plank set into the roof at the far end with a piece of broken but mended glass for a window. When it was very cold, embers from the soldiers' campfire were placed on a bent sheet of iron on the steps in the "reception room" — as Denisov called that part of the dugout — and it became so warm that the officers, of whom there were always some visiting Denisov and Rostov, sat around in their shirtsleeves.

In April, Rostov was on orderly duty. One morning between seven and eight, returning after a sleepless night, he sent for embers, changed his rain-soaked underclothes, said his prayers, drank tea, warmed up, tidied the things on the table and in his corner, and then — his face glowing from the wind, wearing nothing but his shirt — lay on his back with his arms behind his head. He was pleasantly considering the likelihood of a promotion in a few days for his last scouting mission, and was waiting for Denisov, who had gone out somewhere and with whom he wanted to talk.
Suddenly he heard Denisov shouting behind the hut in an agitated, ringing voice. Rostov moved to the window to see who he was talking to and saw the quartermaster, Topchenko.
"I ordered you not to let them eat that Mashka root stuff!" Denisov was shouting. "And I saw with my own eyes how Lazarchuk brought some from the fields."
"I've given the order again and again, your honor, but they won't obey," answered the quartermaster.

Rostov lay back on his bed and thought contentedly: "Let him fuss and bustle — my job's done and I'm lying here. Perfect!" He could hear Lavrushka — Denisov's sly, bold orderly — talking with the quartermaster. Lavrushka was saying something about loaded wagons, biscuits, and oxen he'd seen when out looking for provisions.
Then Denisov's voice was heard shouting further and further away: "Saddle up! Second platoon!"
"Where are they off to now?" thought Rostov.

Five minutes later Denisov came into the hut, climbed with muddy boots onto the bed, lit his pipe, furiously scattered his things about, grabbed his weighted whip, buckled on his saber, and headed out again. When Rostov asked where he was going, he answered vaguely and irritably that he had some business to attend to.

"Let God and our great sovereign judge me afterward!" said Denisov as he went, and Rostov heard the hooves of several horses splashing through the mud. He didn't even bother to find out where Denisov had gone. Having gotten warm in his corner, he fell asleep and didn't leave the hut until evening. Denisov had not yet returned. The weather had cleared up, and near the next hut two officers and a cadet were playing a throwing game, laughing as their stakes buried themselves in the soft mud. Rostov joined them. In the middle of the game, the officers noticed some wagons approaching, with fifteen hussars on their gaunt horses riding behind. The wagons, escorted by the hussars, drew up at the picket ropes, and a crowd of hussars surrounded them.
"There — Denisov's been worrying," said Rostov, "and here are the provisions."
"So they are!" said the officers. "The soldiers will be thrilled!"
A little behind the hussars came Denisov, accompanied by two infantry officers with whom he was arguing.
Rostov went to meet them.
"I'm warning you, Captain," one of the officers — a short, thin man, obviously furious — was saying.
"Haven't I told you I won't give them up?" Denisov replied.
"You'll answer for this, Captain. It's mutiny — seizing your own army's transport. Our men haven't eaten in two days."
"And mine haven't eaten in two weeks," said Denisov.
"It's robbery! You'll answer for it, sir!" said the infantry officer, raising his voice.
"What are you pestering me for?" cried Denisov, suddenly losing his temper. "I'll answer for it, not you — and you'd better clear off before you get hurt. Go! Get out!" he shouted at the officers.
"Very well, then!" shouted the little officer, undaunted and not budging. "If you insist on robbing, I'll —"
"Go to the devil! Quick march, while you're still in one piece!" And Denisov turned his horse on the officer.
"Very well, very well!" muttered the officer threateningly, and turning his horse, he trotted away, bouncing in his saddle.
"A dog on a fence! A real dog on a fence!" shouted Denisov after him — the most insulting thing a cavalryman could say to a mounted infantryman — and riding up to Rostov, he burst out laughing.
"I seized those transports from the infantry by force!" he said. "After all, I can't let our men starve."

The wagons that had reached the hussars had been assigned to an infantry regiment, but when Lavrushka discovered the transport was unguarded, Denisov and his hussars had seized it by force. Biscuits were distributed freely to the soldiers, who even shared them with the other squadrons.
The next day the regimental commander sent for Denisov and, holding his fingers spread in front of his eyes, said:

"This is how I see the matter: I know nothing about it and won't open an investigation. But I advise you to ride to the staff and settle things in the commissariat department — if possible, sign a receipt for the supplies. Otherwise, since the demand was logged against an infantry regiment, there'll be trouble, and the affair could end badly."

From the regimental commander, Denisov rode straight to the staff, sincerely intending to follow this advice. That evening he returned to the dugout in a state Rostov had never seen him in before. Denisov couldn't speak — he was gasping for breath. When Rostov asked what was wrong, he could only manage some incoherent curses and threats in a hoarse, feeble voice.
Alarmed by Denisov's condition, Rostov suggested he undress, drink some water, and send for the doctor.
"Try me for robbery... oh! More water... Let them try me, but I'll always thrash scoundrels... and I'll tell the Emperor... Ice..." he muttered.
The regimental doctor, when he arrived, said bleeding was absolutely necessary. A deep saucer of black blood was drawn from Denisov's hairy arm, and only then could he tell what had happened.

"I get there," Denisov began. "'Where's your chief's office?' They pointed it out. 'Please wait.' 'I've ridden twenty miles and have duties — I can't wait. Announce me.' Very well — so out comes the chief himself, and he decides to lecture me: 'It's robbery!' 'Robbery,' I say, 'is not done by the man who seizes food to feed his soldiers, but by the man who takes it to fill his own pockets!' 'Be quiet!' 'Very well!' Then he says: 'Go give a receipt to the commissary, but your case will be referred to headquarters.' I go to the commissary. I walk in, and at the table — who do you think? No, wait! Who is it that's starving us?" shouted Denisov, slamming his fist on the table so hard it nearly broke and the glasses jumped. "Telyanin! 'What? So it's you who's been starving us? Take this! And this!' And I smashed him right in the face... 'Oh, you... you...' And I started thrashing him... Well, I had some fun, I can tell you!" cried Denisov, gleeful yet furious, his white teeth showing under his black mustache. "I'd have killed him if they hadn't dragged him away!"
"But what are you shouting for? Calm down," said Rostov. "You've opened up your arm again. Wait — let me rebandage it."
Denisov was bandaged up again and put to bed. The next day he woke up calm and cheerful.

But at noon the regimental adjutant came into Rostov and Denisov's dugout with a grave expression and regretfully showed them a document addressed to Major Denisov from the regimental commander, informing them of an inquiry into the previous day's events. The adjutant told them the affair was likely to take a very bad turn: a court-martial had been convened, and given the current severity against marauding and insubordination, demotion to the ranks would be the best Denisov could hope for.

The case, as presented by the complainants, was that Major Denisov, after seizing the transports while drunk, had gone to the chief quartermaster and without provocation called him a thief, threatened to strike him, and when led out had rushed into the office, beaten up two officials, and dislocated one's arm.

When Rostov pressed him with more questions, Denisov said with a laugh that he vaguely recalled some other fellow getting mixed up in it, but that it was all nonsense. He wasn't the least bit worried about any trial, and if those scoundrels dared come at him, he'd give them an answer they wouldn't soon forget.

Denisov talked about the whole thing with contempt, but Rostov knew him too well not to see that — while hiding it from everyone — he was genuinely afraid of the court-martial and worried about the case, which was clearly going badly. Every day brought letters of inquiry and notices from the court, and on the first of May, Denisov was ordered to hand his squadron over to the next in seniority and appear before his division's staff to explain his behavior at the commissariat office. The day before, Platov reconnoitered with two Cossack regiments and two squadrons of hussars. Denisov, as was his habit, rode out in front of the line, showing off his courage. A bullet from a French sharpshooter hit him in the fleshy part of his leg. At any other time Denisov would not have left the regiment for so minor a wound, but now he used it as an excuse to avoid the staff hearing and went to the hospital.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: In June the Battle of Friedland was fought, in which the Pavlograds took no part, and afterward an armistice was declared. Rostov, who felt his friend's absence keenly, having had no news of him since he left and being very anxious about his wound and his legal troubles, took advantage of the armistice to get leave and visit Denisov in the hospital.

The hospital was in a small Prussian town that had been devastated twice by Russian and French troops. Because it was summer, when everything is so beautiful outdoors, the little town looked especially dismal with its broken roofs and fences, its filthy streets, its ragged inhabitants, and the sick and drunken soldiers wandering about.

The hospital occupied a brick building with some of its window frames and panes broken, surrounded by a courtyard enclosed by the remnants of a wooden fence that had been torn apart. Several bandaged soldiers with pale, swollen faces were sitting or walking about in the sunshine in the yard.

The moment Rostov entered the building, he was enveloped by a smell of decay and the stale air of a hospital. On the stairs he met a Russian army doctor smoking a cigar, followed by a Russian assistant.
"I can't tear myself in half," the doctor was saying. "Come to Makar Alexeevich's this evening. I'll be there."
The assistant asked some more questions.
"Oh, do the best you can! What difference does it make?" The doctor noticed Rostov coming up the stairs.
"What do you want, sir?" said the doctor. "What do you want? The bullets spared you — are you here to catch typhus? This place is a death trap, sir."
"How so?" asked Rostov.

"Typhus, sir. Anyone who comes in here dies. Only the two of us — Makeev and I" — he pointed at the assistant — "are still standing. Five doctors have died in this place already. When a new one arrives, he's finished within a week," said the doctor with obvious pride. "Prussian doctors have been invited, but our allies don't care for it at all."
Rostov explained that he wanted to see Major Denisov of the hussars, who had been wounded.

"I have no idea — I can't tell you, sir. Just think! I'm alone in charge of three hospitals with over four hundred patients! It's a good thing the charitable Prussian ladies send us two pounds of coffee and some lint each month, or we'd be done for!" he laughed. "Four hundred, sir, and they keep sending me fresh ones. There are four hundred, aren't there?" he asked, turning to the assistant.
The assistant looked exhausted — clearly irritated and waiting for the chatty doctor to leave.
"Major Denisov," Rostov said again. "He was wounded at Molliten."
"Dead, I think. Eh, Makeev?" the doctor asked indifferently.
The assistant, however, did not confirm the doctor's words.
"Is he tall and with reddish hair?" asked the doctor.
Rostov described Denisov's appearance.
"There was one like that," said the doctor, sounding pleased. "That one's dead, I think. But I'll check our list. We had a list. Do you have it, Makeev?"
"Makar Alexeevich has the list," the assistant answered. "But if you go to the officers' ward, you'll see for yourself," he added, turning to Rostov.
"Better not, sir," said the doctor. "You might end up staying here yourself."
But Rostov politely excused himself from the doctor and asked the assistant to show him the way.
"Just don't blame me!" the doctor shouted after him.

Rostov and the assistant entered the dark corridor. The smell was so overpowering there that Rostov had to hold his nose and stop to gather himself before going on. A door opened on the right, and a gaunt, sallow man on crutches — barefoot, wearing only his underclothes — limped out and, leaning against the doorframe, stared with glittering, envious eyes at the people passing by. Glancing through the door, Rostov saw sick and wounded men lying on the floor on straw and overcoats.
"May I go in and look?"
"What's there to see?" said the assistant.

But precisely because the assistant obviously didn't want him to go in, Rostov entered the soldiers' ward. The foul air, which he'd already started getting used to in the corridor, was even stronger here — different, more acrid — and one could tell this was where it originated.

In the long room, brightly lit by sun through the large windows, the sick and wounded lay in two rows with their heads against the walls, leaving a passage down the middle. Most were unconscious and took no notice of the visitors. Those who were awake raised themselves or lifted their thin, yellow faces, all staring at Rostov with the same expression — hope, relief, reproach, and envy of someone else's health. Rostov walked to the center of the room and through the open doors saw the same scene in the two rooms beyond. He stopped and looked around in silence. He had not expected anything like this. Right in front of him, almost blocking the passage on the bare floor, lay a sick man — probably a Cossack, judging by his haircut. The man lay on his back, his massive arms and legs stretched out. His face was purple, his eyes rolled back until only the whites showed, and on his bare legs and arms — still red — the veins stood out like cords. He was knocking the back of his head against the floor, hoarsely repeating a single word over and over. Rostov listened and made it out. It was: "Drink... drink... a drink!" Rostov looked around for someone to help this man back to his place and bring him water.
"Who looks after the sick here?" he asked the assistant.
Just then a commissariat soldier — a hospital orderly — marched stiffly in from the next room and drew himself up in front of Rostov.
"Good day, your honor!" he shouted, rolling his eyes at Rostov, evidently taking him for a hospital official.
"Get this man to his place and bring him water," said Rostov, pointing to the Cossack.
"Yes, your honor," the soldier replied with gusto, rolling his eyes even more and standing even straighter — but not moving.

"No — nothing can be done here," thought Rostov, lowering his eyes. He was about to leave when he became aware of an intense gaze fixed on him from the right. He turned. Near the corner, sitting on an overcoat, was an old, unshaven, gray-bearded soldier, thin as a skeleton, with a stern sallow face and eyes locked on Rostov. The man's neighbor on one side was whispering something to him, pointing at Rostov. The old man clearly wanted to speak. Rostov moved closer and saw that the man had only one leg bent beneath him — the other had been amputated above the knee. His neighbor on the other side, who lay motionless at some distance with his head thrown back, was a young soldier with a snub nose. His pale, waxy face was still freckled, and his eyes were rolled back. Rostov looked at the young soldier and felt a cold chill run down his spine.
"Why, this one seems..." he began, turning to the assistant.
"We've been begging and begging, your honor," said the old soldier, his jaw trembling. "He's been dead since this morning. We're men after all, not dogs."
"I'll send someone right away. He'll be removed — removed immediately," said the assistant quickly. "Let's go, your honor."
"Yes, yes, let's go," said Rostov hastily, and with lowered eyes, trying to make himself invisible, he hurried between the rows of reproachful, envious eyes fixed on him, and escaped from the room.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: The assistant led Rostov along the corridor to the officers' wards, which consisted of three rooms with open doors. These rooms had actual beds, and the sick and wounded officers were lying or sitting on them. Some walked about in hospital gowns. The first person Rostov met in the officers' ward was a thin little man with one arm, walking around the first room in a nightcap and hospital gown, a pipe clenched between his teeth. Rostov looked at him, trying to remember where he'd seen him before.

"Look where we've met again!" said the little man. "Tushin — Tushin! Don't you remember? I gave you a ride at Schon Grabern. And I've had a bit taken off, you see..." he went on with a smile, pointing to the empty sleeve of his gown. "Looking for Vasili Dmitrich Denisov? He's my neighbor. Here, this way." And Tushin led him to the next room, from which came the sound of several laughing voices.

"How can they laugh — or even go on living — in a place like this?" thought Rostov, still aware of the stench of dead flesh from the soldiers' ward, still feeling those envious stares following him out, still seeing the face of that young soldier with his rolled-back eyes.
Denisov lay asleep on his bed with his head under the blanket, though it was nearly noon.

"Wostov! How are you, how are you?" he called out in the same voice as at the regiment — but Rostov noticed sadly that beneath this familiar ease and energy, something new, sinister, and hidden showed in Denisov's expression and tone.

His wound, though slight, still hadn't healed even now, six weeks after being hit. His face had the same swollen pallor as the other patients', but that wasn't what struck Rostov. What struck him was that Denisov didn't seem glad to see him and smiled unnaturally. He didn't ask about the regiment or the general state of things, and when Rostov brought them up, he didn't listen.

Rostov even noticed that Denisov didn't like being reminded of the regiment or of that other free life going on outside the hospital. He seemed to be trying to forget all that, and was only interested in his case against the commissariat officials. When Rostov asked about the case, Denisov immediately produced papers from under his pillow — the commission's letter and his draft reply — and grew animated as he read, particularly drawing Rostov's attention to the biting retorts he'd aimed at his enemies. His hospital companions, who had gathered around Rostov as a fresh arrival from the outside world, gradually drifted away as soon as Denisov began reading. Rostov could tell from their faces that they had all heard this story many times before and were tired of it. Only the man in the next bed — a stout Uhlan — kept sitting on his bed, gloomily frowning and smoking his pipe, and little one-armed Tushin went on listening, shaking his head disapprovingly. In the middle of the reading, the Uhlan spoke up.
"What I say is," he said, turning to Rostov, "it would be best to simply petition the Emperor for pardon. They say big rewards are being handed out now — surely a pardon would be granted."

"Me — petition the Empewo'!" exclaimed Denisov in a voice that tried hard to recover its old fire but came out sounding like impotent irritation. "What for? If I were a wobber I'd ask for mercy, but I'm being court-martialed for bwinging wobbers to justice. Let them twy me — I'm not afwaid of anyone. I've served the Tsar and my countwy honowably and have not stolen! And am I to be degwaded? Listen, I'm w'iting to them stwaight: 'If I had wobbed the Tweasuwy...'"

"It's certainly well written," said Tushin, "but that's not the point, Vasili Dmitrich." He too turned to Rostov. "You have to submit, and Vasili Dmitrich won't do it. The auditor told you it was a bad business."
"Well, let it be bad," said Denisov.

"The auditor wrote out a petition for you," Tushin continued, "and you should sign it and ask this gentleman to deliver it. No doubt he" — indicating Rostov — "has connections at headquarters. You won't find a better chance."
"Haven't I said I'm not going to gwovel?" Denisov interrupted, and went back to reading his paper.

Rostov didn't have the heart to press Denisov, though he instinctively felt that the path advised by Tushin and the other officers was the safest, and would have been glad to help. He knew Denisov's stubborn will and fierce, impetuous temperament.

When the reading of Denisov's scathing reply — which took over an hour — was finished, Rostov said nothing. He spent the rest of the day in a deeply glum state among Denisov's hospital companions, telling them what he knew and listening to their stories. Denisov was moody and silent all evening.
Late that evening, when Rostov was about to leave, he asked Denisov if he had any messages for him.
"Yes — wait a moment," said Denisov, glancing around at the officers. He took his papers from under his pillow and went to the window where there was an inkpot, and sat down to write.

"It seems there's no point banging your head against a wall!" he said, coming from the window and handing Rostov a large envelope. Inside was the petition to the Emperor that the auditor had drafted, in which Denisov — without mentioning the commissariat officials' offenses — simply asked for a pardon.
"Hand it in. It seems..."
He didn't finish, but gave a painfully unnatural smile.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: Having returned to the regiment and told the commander about Denisov's situation, Rostov rode to Tilsit with the letter to the Emperor.
On the thirteenth of June, the French and Russian Emperors arrived in Tilsit. Boris Drubetskoy had asked the important personage he served to include him in the suite for the Tilsit visit.
"I'd like to see the great man," he said, referring to Napoleon — whom until now he, like everyone else, had always called Buonaparte.
"You are speaking of Buonaparte?" asked the general with a smile.
Boris looked at the general inquiringly and instantly realized he was being tested.
"I am speaking, Prince, of the Emperor Napoleon," he replied. The general patted him on the shoulder with a smile.
"You will go far," he said, and took him along to Tilsit.

Boris was among the few present on the banks of the Niemen on the day the two Emperors met. He saw the raft decorated with monograms, saw Napoleon pass before the French Guards on the far bank, saw the thoughtful face of Emperor Alexander as he sat silently in a tavern on the riverbank awaiting Napoleon's arrival, and watched both Emperors board their boats and meet on the raft — Napoleon stepping forward quickly to greet Alexander and extending his hand — before they both disappeared into the pavilion. Since entering the highest circles, Boris had made it his habit to observe everything carefully and note it down. At the time of the Tilsit meeting, he asked about the names and uniforms of Napoleon's entourage and listened closely to every word spoken by important people. When the Emperors entered the pavilion, he checked his watch and remembered to check it again when Alexander emerged. The meeting had lasted one hour and fifty-three minutes. He recorded this that same evening among other facts he considered historically significant. Since the Emperor's suite was very small, being present at Tilsit for this interview was a matter of great importance for anyone who valued his career. Boris, having secured this advantage, felt his position was now firmly established. He had not only become known — people had grown used to him and accepted him. Twice he had carried out missions for the Emperor himself, so that the sovereign knew his face, and everyone at court, far from giving him the cold shoulder as they had at first when they considered him a newcomer, would now have been surprised had he been absent.

Boris was lodging with another aide-de-camp, the Polish Count Zhilinski. Zhilinski, a Pole raised in Paris, was rich, passionately pro-French, and nearly every day of their stay in Tilsit, French Guard officers and men from French headquarters dined and lunched with him and Boris.

On the evening of the twenty-fourth of June, Count Zhilinski arranged a supper for his French friends. The guest of honor was one of Napoleon's aides-de-camp; there were also several French Guard officers and a page of Napoleon's — a young man from an old aristocratic French family. That same day, Rostov — slipping into Tilsit in civilian clothes under cover of darkness to avoid being recognized — made his way to the quarters shared by Boris and Zhilinski.

Rostov, like the whole army he came from, was far from feeling the shift in attitude toward Napoleon and the French — enemies who had suddenly become friends — that had occurred at headquarters and in Boris's world. In the army, Bonaparte and the French were still regarded with a mix of anger, contempt, and fear. Just recently, talking with one of Platov's Cossack officers, Rostov had argued that if Napoleon were captured, he should be treated not as a sovereign but as a criminal. Quite recently, meeting a wounded French colonel on the road, Rostov had insisted heatedly that peace was impossible between a legitimate ruler and the criminal Bonaparte. He was therefore unpleasantly startled to find French officers in Boris's quarters, wearing uniforms he had only ever seen from the far side of the battle lines. The moment he glimpsed a French officer poking his head out the door, that combative hostility he always felt at the sight of the enemy seized him. He stopped at the threshold and asked in Russian whether Drubetskoy lived there. Boris, hearing an unfamiliar voice in the entry, came out to meet him. A flash of annoyance crossed his face when he first recognized Rostov.
"Ah, it's you? Very glad — very glad to see you," he said, however, coming toward him with a smile. But Rostov had caught his first reaction.
"I've come at a bad time, I think. I shouldn't have come, but I have business," he said coldly.
"No — I only wonder how you got away from your regiment. I'll be with you in a moment," he said (in French), answering someone who called him.
* Dans un moment je suis à vous.
"I see I'm intruding," Rostov repeated.

The look of annoyance had already vanished from Boris's face. Having apparently considered and decided how to handle things, he took both of Rostov's hands very calmly and led him into the next room. His eyes, looking steadily at Rostov, seemed somehow veiled — as if screened by blue spectacles of social propriety. So it seemed to Rostov.

"Oh, come now! As if you could come at a wrong time!" said Boris, and he led him into the room where the supper table was laid and introduced him to his guests, explaining that Rostov was not a civilian but a hussar officer and an old friend.
"Count Zhilinski — le Comte N.N. — le Capitaine S.S.," he said, naming the guests. Rostov looked at the Frenchmen with a scowl, bowed reluctantly, and said nothing.

Zhilinski clearly did not welcome this new Russian into his circle and didn't speak to Rostov. Boris seemed not to notice the strain the newcomer created, and with his usual pleasant composure and the same veiled look in his eyes, tried to keep the conversation going. One of the Frenchmen, with the characteristic politeness of his countrymen, addressed the stubbornly silent Rostov, suggesting he had probably come to Tilsit to see the Emperor.
"No — I came on business," Rostov replied curtly.

Rostov had been in a bad mood from the moment he noticed Boris's displeasure, and as always happens when one is out of sorts, everyone seemed to regard him with aversion and he felt in the way everywhere. And he really was in their way — he was the only one not taking part in the conversation, which had resumed. The glances his fellow guests cast at him seemed to say: "What's he doing here?" He stood up and went over to Boris.
"I'm in your way," he said quietly. "Come talk about my business, and I'll leave."
"Oh no, not at all," said Boris. "But if you're tired, come lie down in my room and rest."
"Yes, really..."

They went into the small room where Boris slept. Rostov, without sitting down, launched immediately — irritably, as if Boris were somehow to blame — into the story of Denisov's case, asking whether Boris could and would use his connections to intercede with the Emperor on Denisov's behalf and deliver the petition. Being alone with Boris, Rostov felt for the first time that he couldn't look him in the eye without discomfort. Boris, one leg crossed over the other, stroking the slender fingers of his right hand with his left, listened to Rostov the way a general listens to a subordinate's report — now looking aside, now gazing straight into Rostov's eyes with that same veiled expression. Each time this happened, Rostov felt awkward and dropped his gaze.

"I've heard of such cases, and I know His Majesty is very strict in these matters. I think it would be best not to bring it before the Emperor but to apply to the corps commander. But in general, I think..."
"So you don't want to do anything? Just say so!" Rostov almost shouted, not looking Boris in the face.
Boris smiled.
"On the contrary — I'll do what I can. Only I thought..."
At that moment Zhilinski's voice called Boris from the other room.

"Well, go then — go, go..." said Rostov, and declining supper, he stayed alone in the little room, pacing back and forth for a long time, listening to the lighthearted French conversation coming from next door.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: Rostov had come to Tilsit on the worst possible day for delivering a petition on Denisov's behalf. He couldn't go to the general himself, being in civilian clothes and having come to Tilsit without permission; and Boris, even had he wanted to, couldn't have done anything the following day either. On that day — June 27 — the peace preliminaries were signed. The Emperors exchanged decorations: Alexander received the Cross of the Legion of Honor and Napoleon the Order of Saint Andrew of the First Degree. A dinner had been arranged for that evening, given by a battalion of the French Guards for the Preobrazhensky battalion. The Emperors were to attend.

Rostov felt so ill at ease with Boris that when Boris looked in after supper, he pretended to be asleep. Early the next morning he left, avoiding Boris. In civilian clothes and a round hat, he wandered through the town, staring at the French and their uniforms and at the streets and buildings where the Russian and French Emperors were staying. In a square he saw tables being set up and preparations underway for the dinner; he saw Russian and French flags draped across the streets with huge monograms A and N. The windows of the houses also displayed flags and bunting.

"Boris doesn't want to help me, and I don't want to ask him. That's settled," Nicholas thought. "It's all over between us, but I won't leave without doing everything I can for Denisov — and certainly not without getting his letter to the Emperor. The Emperor! He's right here!" thought Rostov, who had unconsciously wandered back to the house where Alexander was staying.
Saddled horses stood before the building and the suite was assembling, evidently preparing for the Emperor to come out.

"I could see him at any moment," thought Rostov. "If only I could hand the letter to him directly and tell him everything... Would they really arrest me for being in civilian clothes? Surely not! He would understand who is in the right. He understands everything, knows everything. Who could be more just, more generous than he? And even if they did arrest me for being here — what would it matter?" he thought, looking at an officer entering the Emperor's residence. "People go in all the time. It's all nonsense! I'll go in and give the letter to the Emperor myself — so much the worse for Drubetskoy, who's driven me to it!" And with a resolve that surprised even himself, Rostov felt for the letter in his pocket and went straight to the house.

"No — I won't miss my chance this time, the way I did after Austerlitz," he thought, expecting at any moment to encounter the sovereign and feeling the blood rush to his heart at the thought. "I'll fall at his feet and beg him. He'll raise me up, listen, and even thank me. 'I am happy when I can do good, but to right an injustice is the greatest happiness,'" Rostov imagined the sovereign saying. And ignoring the curious stares of passersby, he entered the porch of the Emperor's residence.
A broad staircase led straight up from the entrance, and to the right he saw a closed door. Below, under the staircase, was a door to the lower floor.
"Whom do you want?" someone asked.
"To deliver a letter — a petition — to His Majesty," said Nicholas, his voice trembling.
"A petition? This way, to the officer on duty" — he was shown the door leading downstairs — "only it won't be accepted."

Hearing this indifferent voice, Rostov was struck with fear at what he was doing. The thought of encountering the Emperor at any moment was thrilling and therefore terrifying, and he was ready to bolt. But the official who had questioned him opened the door, and Rostov walked in.

A short, stocky man of about thirty, in white breeches, high boots, and a fine batiste shirt he had obviously just put on, stood in the room while his valet buttoned a new pair of handsome silk-embroidered suspenders onto the back of his breeches — which, for some reason, caught Rostov's attention. This man was speaking to someone in the next room.
"A good figure and in her first bloom," he was saying — but on seeing Rostov, he stopped and frowned.
"What is it? A petition?"
"What is it?" asked the person in the other room.
"Another petitioner," answered the man with the suspenders.
"Tell him to come back later. He'll be coming out soon — we need to go."
"Later... later! Tomorrow. It's too late..."
Rostov turned to leave, but the man in the suspenders stopped him.
"Who sent you? Who are you?"
"I come from Major Denisov," answered Rostov.
"Are you an officer?"
"Lieutenant Count Rostov."
"What nerve! Submit it through your commander. Now get along with you — go!" And he went back to putting on the uniform his valet was handing him.
Rostov went back into the hall and realized that the porch was now crowded with officers and generals in full dress uniform, through whom he had to pass.

Cursing his own audacity, his heart sinking at the thought of coming face to face with the Emperor and being humiliated and arrested in his presence — fully aware now of how improper his conduct was and regretting it — Rostov, with downcast eyes, was making his way out through the glittering suite when a familiar voice called him and a hand seized his arm.
"What are you doing here in civilian dress, sir?" asked a deep voice.
It was a cavalry general who had earned the Emperor's special favor during this campaign and who had previously commanded the division in which Rostov served.

Rostov began stammering an excuse, but seeing the general's kind, good-humored face, he pulled him aside and in an excited voice told him the whole story, begging him to intercede for Denisov, whom the general knew. After hearing him out, the general shook his head gravely.
"I'm sorry — sorry for the fine fellow. Give me the letter."

Barely had Rostov handed over the letter and finished explaining Denisov's case when hurried footsteps and the jingle of spurs were heard on the stairs, and the general, leaving him, went to the porch. The gentlemen of the Emperor's suite ran down the stairs to their horses. Hayne, the same groom who had been at Austerlitz, led up the Emperor's horse, and the faint creak of a footstep Rostov recognized at once sounded on the stairs. Forgetting the danger of being recognized, Rostov moved close to the porch with some curious civilians, and once again — after two years — he saw the features he adored: the same face, the same gaze, the same step, the same blend of majesty and gentleness. The feeling of enthusiasm and love for his sovereign rose again in Rostov's soul with all its old force. In his Preobrazhensky uniform — white leather breeches and high boots — wearing a star Rostov didn't recognize (it was the Legion of Honor), the sovereign came out onto the porch, pulling on his gloves and carrying his hat under his arm. He paused, looked around, and his glance seemed to brighten everything it touched. He spoke a few words to some generals, and recognizing the former commander of Rostov's division, smiled and beckoned him over.
The whole suite drew back, and Rostov saw the general talking with the Emperor for some time.

The Emperor said a few words and then stepped toward his horse. Again the crowd of courtiers and onlookers (Rostov among them) moved closer. Stopping beside his horse with one hand on the saddle, the Emperor turned to the cavalry general and said in a loud voice, clearly intending to be heard by all:
"I cannot do it, General. I cannot — because the law is stronger than I." And he put his foot in the stirrup.
The general bowed respectfully, and the sovereign mounted and rode off down the street at a gallop. Beside himself with emotion, Rostov ran after him with the crowd.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: The Emperor rode to the square where a battalion of the Preobrazhensky regiment stood on one side, facing a battalion of the French Guards in their bearskin caps on the other.

As the Tsar approached one end of the line, another group of horsemen galloped up from the opposite direction, and at their head Rostov recognized Napoleon. It could be no one else. He came at a gallop wearing a small hat, a blue uniform open over a white vest, and the Saint Andrew ribbon across his shoulder. He rode a superb gray Arab horse with a crimson, gold-embroidered saddlecloth. Approaching Alexander, he raised his hat, and as he did so, Rostov — with his cavalryman's eye — couldn't help noticing that Napoleon didn't sit well or firmly in the saddle. The battalions shouted "Hurrah!" and "Vive l'Empereur!" Napoleon said something to Alexander, and both Emperors dismounted and took each other's hands. Napoleon's face wore an unpleasant, artificial smile. Alexander was saying something pleasant to him.

Despite the trampling of the French gendarmes' horses, which were pushing back the crowd, Rostov kept his eyes on every movement of both Alexander and Bonaparte. He was struck to see Alexander treating Bonaparte as an equal, and that Napoleon was completely at ease with the Tsar, as though such encounters with an Emperor were an everyday matter for him.

Alexander and Napoleon, with their long trains of attendants, approached the right side of the Preobrazhensky battalion and came straight up to the crowd. The crowd unexpectedly found itself so close to the Emperors that Rostov, standing in the front row, was afraid he might be recognized.
"Sire, I ask your permission to present the Legion of Honor to the bravest of your soldiers," said a sharp, precise voice, articulating every letter.
It was the short Napoleon, looking straight up into Alexander's eyes. Alexander listened attentively, then bent his head and smiled pleasantly.

"To the one who bore himself most bravely in this last war," Napoleon added, emphasizing each syllable, and with a composure that irritated Rostov, he ran his eyes over the Russian ranks drawn up before him — every soldier standing at attention, eyes fixed on their Emperor.
"Will Your Majesty allow me to consult the colonel?" said Alexander, and he took a few quick steps toward Prince Kozlovsky, the battalion commander.
Meanwhile, Bonaparte began pulling the glove off his small white hand, tore it in the process, and threw it away. An aide-de-camp behind him scrambled to pick it up.
"To whom shall it be given?" Emperor Alexander asked Kozlovsky in Russian, in a low voice.
"To whomever Your Majesty commands."
The Emperor knit his brows with displeasure and, glancing back, remarked:
"But we must give him an answer."
Kozlovsky scanned the ranks with a resolute eye, and his gaze swept over Rostov.
"Can it be me?" thought Rostov.
"Lazarev!" the colonel called, frowning, and Lazarev, the first soldier in the rank, stepped briskly forward.

"Where are you going? Stay here!" voices whispered to Lazarev, who didn't know where to go. He stopped, casting an anxious sidelong glance at his colonel. His face twitched, as often happens to soldiers called before the ranks.

Napoleon slightly turned his head and reached his plump little hand behind him, as if to take something. His suite, instantly guessing what he wanted, whispered and passed something from hand to hand, and a page — the same one Rostov had seen the night before at Boris's — ran forward, bowed respectfully over the outstretched hand, and without a moment's delay placed an Order on a red ribbon into it. Napoleon, without looking, pressed two fingers together and held the medal between them. Then he approached Lazarev — who kept rolling his eyes and staring stubbornly at his own sovereign — glanced at Emperor Alexander as if to say that what he was about to do was done for the sake of his ally, and his small white hand, holding the Order, touched one of Lazarev's buttons. It was as if Napoleon knew that the mere touch of his hand on this soldier's chest would make the man forever happy, singled out from all the rest of humanity. Napoleon simply laid the cross on Lazarev's breast and, dropping his hand, turned toward Alexander — certain the cross would stay in place. And it did.

Eager hands — Russian and French — immediately seized the medal and pinned it to the uniform. Lazarev glanced sullenly at the little man with white hands who was doing something to him, and still standing motionless at attention, looked straight at Alexander again — as if asking whether he should stay there, or leave, or do something else. But receiving no orders, he remained frozen in that rigid position for some time.
The Emperors remounted and rode away. The Preobrazhensky battalion broke ranks and mingled with the French Guards, and they sat down together at the tables that had been prepared.

Lazarev sat in the place of honor. Russian and French officers embraced him, congratulated him, and shook his hand. Crowds of officers and civilians gathered just to look at him. A hum of Russian and French voices and laughter filled the square around the tables. Two officers with flushed, happy faces walked past Rostov.
"What do you think of the feast? All on silver plate!" one of them was saying. "Have you seen Lazarev?"
"I have."
"Tomorrow, I hear, the Preobrazhenskis are hosting the French."
"Yes, but what luck for Lazarev! Twelve hundred francs a year for life."
"Here's a cap, boys!" shouted a Preobrazhensky soldier, pulling on a shaggy French cap.
"That's a fine thing! First-rate!"

"Have you heard the password?" one Guards officer asked another. "The day before yesterday it was 'Napoleon, France, bravoure'; yesterday, 'Alexandre, Russie, grandeur.' One day our Emperor gives it, the next day Napoleon. Tomorrow our Emperor will send a Saint George's Cross to the bravest of the French Guards. Has to be done — he must reciprocate."
Boris, together with his friend Zhilinski, also came to watch the Preobrazhensky banquet. On his way back he spotted Rostov standing by the corner of a building.
"Rostov! How are you? We missed each other," he said — and couldn't help asking what was wrong, so strangely gloomy and troubled was Rostov's face.
"Nothing, nothing," Rostov replied.
"You'll come by?"
"Yes, I will."

Rostov stood at that corner for a long time, watching the feast from afar. A painful process was working itself out in his mind, one he couldn't bring to a conclusion. Terrible doubts rose in his soul. He remembered Denisov with his altered expression, his submission, and the whole hospital — arms and legs torn off, filth and disease. So vividly did he recall the hospital stench of dead flesh that he looked around to find where the smell was coming from. Then he thought of that self-satisfied Bonaparte with his small white hands, who was now an Emperor — liked and respected by Alexander. Then why the severed limbs and the dead? Then his mind jumped to Lazarev rewarded while Denisov was punished and unforgiven. He caught himself thinking such strange thoughts that he frightened himself.

The smell of the food the Preobrazhenskis were eating and a pang of hunger brought him back. He had to eat something before leaving. He went to a hotel he had noticed that morning. He found it so packed with people — including officers who, like himself, had come in civilian clothes — that he could barely get a table. Two officers from his own division joined him. The conversation naturally turned to the peace. The officers, like most of the army, were unhappy with the peace concluded after Friedland. They said if Russia had held out a bit longer, Napoleon would have been finished — his troops had neither food nor ammunition. Nicholas ate and drank (mainly drank) in silence. He finished two bottles of wine by himself. The process in his mind went on tormenting him without reaching resolution. He feared to give in to his thoughts, yet couldn't shake them. Suddenly, when one of the officers said it was humiliating to look at the French, Rostov erupted with an uncalled-for fury that startled everyone:
"How can you judge what's best?" he cried, blood rushing to his face. "How can you judge the Emperor's actions? What right do we have to argue? We can't comprehend the Emperor's aims or his actions!"
"But I never said anything about the Emperor!" said the officer, defending himself, unable to explain Rostov's outburst except by assuming he was drunk.
But Rostov wasn't listening.

"We're not diplomats — we're soldiers, nothing more," he went on. "If we're ordered to die, we die. If we're punished, it means we deserve it. It's not for us to judge. If the Emperor sees fit to recognize Bonaparte as Emperor and make an alliance with him, then that's the right thing to do. If we start judging and arguing about everything, nothing will be sacred! Next we'll be saying there is no God — nothing!" shouted Nicholas, banging the table — very little to the point as far as his listeners could tell, but perfectly relevant to the train of his own thoughts.
"Our job is to do our duty — to fight, not to think! That's all," he said.
"And to drink," said one of the officers, not wanting a quarrel.
"Yes, and to drink," Nicholas agreed. "Hey there! Another bottle!" he shouted.
In 1808 Emperor Alexander went to Erfurt for another meeting with Emperor Napoleon, and in the upper circles of Petersburg there was much talk of the grandeur of this important occasion.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: In 1809, the intimacy between "the world's two arbiters," as Napoleon and Alexander were called, had become so close that when Napoleon declared war on Austria, a Russian corps crossed the frontier to fight alongside their old enemy Bonaparte against their old ally the Austrian Emperor, and at court people even spoke of a possible marriage between Napoleon and one of Alexander's sisters. But besides foreign policy, Russian society's attention was keenly focused on the internal reforms being carried out across all branches of government.

Life, meanwhile — real life, with its essential concerns of health and sickness, work and rest, and its intellectual pursuits of thought, science, poetry, music, love, friendship, hatred, and passion — went on as usual, independently of and apart from political friendship or enmity with Napoleon Bonaparte, and from all the grand schemes of reform.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Prince Andrew had spent two years continuously in the country.

All the plans Pierre had attempted on his estates — constantly switching from one thing to another without finishing any of them — were carried out by Prince Andrew quietly and without apparent effort.
He possessed to the highest degree a practical tenacity that Pierre lacked, and without fuss or strain this quality set things in motion.

On one of his estates, three hundred serfs were liberated and became free agricultural laborers — one of the first such examples in Russia. On other estates, the serfs' compulsory labor was replaced by a cash payment. A trained midwife was hired for Bogucharovo at his expense, and a priest was paid to teach the peasants' and household serfs' children reading and writing.

Prince Andrew spent half his time at Bald Hills with his father and his son, who was still in the care of nurses. The other half he spent in "Bogucharovo Cloister," as his father called Prince Andrew's estate. Despite the indifference to the world's affairs he had professed to Pierre, he diligently followed everything that was happening. He received many books and was surprised to find that when visitors came from Petersburg — the very center of life — they were actually behind him, despite his never leaving the country, in their knowledge of both domestic and foreign affairs.

Besides managing his estates and reading widely, Prince Andrew was at this time working on a critical analysis of the two most recent, unsuccessful campaigns and drafting a proposal for reforming the army's rules and regulations.
In the spring of 1809 he went to visit the Ryazan estates that his son had inherited and of which he was guardian.

Warmed by the spring sunshine, he sat in the open carriage looking at the new grass, the first leaves on the birch trees, and the first puffs of white cloud floating across the clear blue sky. He wasn't thinking about anything in particular, but gazed around cheerfully and absent-mindedly.

They crossed the ferry where he had talked with Pierre the year before. They went through the muddy village, past threshing floors and green fields of winter rye, downhill where snow still lingered near the bridge, uphill where the clay had been liquefied by rain, past strips of stubble and bushes touched with green here and there, and into a birch forest that lined both sides of the road. In the forest it was almost hot — no wind could be felt. The birches with their sticky green leaves stood motionless, and lilac flowers and the first blades of green grass pushed up through last year's fallen leaves. The dark evergreen of the small fir trees scattered among the birches was an unwelcome reminder of winter. Entering the forest, the horses began to snort and broke into a visible sweat.
Peter, the footman, said something to the coachman; the latter agreed. But apparently the coachman's agreement wasn't enough for Peter, who turned on the box toward his master.
"How pleasant it is, your excellency!" he said with a respectful smile.
"What?"
"It's pleasant, your excellency!"

"What is he talking about?" thought Prince Andrew. "Oh — the spring, I suppose," he thought, glancing around. "Yes, everything is green already. How early! The birches, the cherry trees, and the alders too are coming out. But the oaks show no sign yet. Ah — there's one!"

At the edge of the road stood an oak. Probably ten times the age of the birch trees that formed the forest, it was ten times as thick and twice as tall. It was an enormous tree, its girth twice what a man could embrace, and clearly long ago some of its branches had been broken off and its bark scarred. With its huge, ungainly limbs sprawling asymmetrically, its gnarled hands and fingers, it stood like an aged, stern, scornful giant among the smiling birch trees. Only the dead-looking evergreen firs scattered through the forest and this oak refused to yield to the charm of spring or acknowledge either the sunshine or the season.

"Spring, love, happiness!" this oak seemed to say. "Aren't you tired of that stupid, meaningless, endlessly repeated fraud? Always the same, and always a sham. There is no spring, no sun, no happiness! Look at those stunted dead firs — always the same. And look at me, sticking out my broken and scarred limbs wherever they've grown — from my back, from my sides. As they grew, so I stand — and I don't believe in your hopes and your lies."

As he drove through the forest, Prince Andrew turned several times to look at that oak, as if expecting something from it. Under the oak too there were flowers and grass, but it stood among them scowling, rigid, misshapen, and grim as ever.
"Yes, the oak is right — a thousand times right," thought Prince Andrew. "Let others — the young — fall for that fraud again, but we know life. Our life is finished!"

A whole sequence of new thoughts — hopeless but strangely pleasant in their melancholy — rose in his mind in connection with that tree. During this journey he reconsidered his life, as it were, from scratch, and arrived at his old conclusion — comforting in its hopelessness: that there was nothing for him to begin, that he must simply live out his days, content to do no harm, and not troubling himself or wishing for anything.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Prince Andrew needed to see the district marshal of the nobility in connection with his son's Ryazan estate. This marshal was Count Ilya Rostov, and in the middle of May, Prince Andrew went to visit him.
It was now hot spring weather. The forest was fully green. It was dusty and so warm that passing any water made you long to bathe.

Prince Andrew, preoccupied and gloomy about the business he needed to discuss with the marshal, was driving up the avenue to the Rostovs' house at Otradnoe. He heard merry girlish cries from behind some trees to the right and saw a group of girls running across the path of his carriage. Ahead of the others, nearest to him, ran a dark-haired, remarkably slim, pretty girl in a yellow cotton dress with a white kerchief on her head, from under which loose locks of hair had escaped. The girl was shouting something but, seeing a stranger, ran back laughing without looking at him.

Suddenly, and he didn't know why, he felt a pang. The day was so beautiful, the sun so bright, everything around so cheerful — and that slim, pretty girl didn't know or care that he existed. She was content and happy in her own separate — probably silly — but bright and joyful life. "What is she so glad about? What is she thinking of? Not about military regulations or the arrangement of the Ryazan serfs' rents. What is she thinking? Why is she so happy?" Prince Andrew asked himself with involuntary curiosity.

In 1809 Count Ilya Rostov was living at Otradnoe just as in previous years — entertaining nearly the whole province with hunts, theatricals, dinners, and music. He was glad to see Prince Andrew, as he was to see any new visitor, and insisted he stay the night.

During the tedious day, in the course of which he was entertained by his elderly hosts and the more important visitors — the old count's house was packed in anticipation of a name-day celebration — Prince Andrew kept glancing at Natasha, who was gay and laughing among the younger guests, and each time he asked himself: "What is she thinking about? Why is she so happy?"

That night, alone in unfamiliar surroundings, he was long unable to sleep. He read for a while, then put out his candle — then relit it. It was hot in the room, with the shutters closed. He was annoyed at the foolish old man (as he called Rostov) who had kept him there by insisting that some necessary documents hadn't arrived from town, and he was annoyed at himself for having stayed.

He got up and went to the window to open it. The moment he opened the shutters, the moonlight — as if it had been waiting for this — flooded into the room. He opened the casement. The night was cool, bright, and perfectly still. Just below the window stood a row of pollard trees, black on one side, silvery on the other. Beneath them grew some kind of lush, wet, bushy vegetation with silver-touched leaves and stems here and there. Further off, beyond the dark trees, a roof glistened with dew; to the right rose a great leafy tree with brilliantly white trunk and branches, and above it shone the moon, nearly full, in a pale, almost starless spring sky. Prince Andrew leaned his elbows on the window ledge and let his gaze rest on that sky.
His room was on the first floor. Those in the rooms above were awake too. He heard female voices overhead.
"Just once more," said a girlish voice above him that Prince Andrew recognized at once.
"But when are you going to bed?" replied another voice.
"I won't! I can't sleep — what's the use? Come on, one last time."
Two girlish voices sang a musical passage — the ending of some song.
"Oh, how lovely! Now go to sleep — that's it."

"You go to sleep, but I can't," said the first voice, coming nearer to the window. She was evidently leaning right out, because the rustle of her dress and even her breathing could be heard. Everything was stone-still — like the moon and its light and the shadows. Prince Andrew, too, dared not stir, afraid of revealing his presence.

"Sonya! Sonya!" he heard the first voice again. "Oh, how can you sleep! Just look how gorgeous it is! Oh, how gorgeous! Wake up, Sonya!" she said, almost in tears. "There has never, never been such a beautiful night!"
Sonya murmured something reluctant in reply.

"Come look at the moon! Oh, how lovely! Come here, darling, sweetheart, come here! See? I feel like crouching down on my heels and hugging my knees like this, pulling tight — as tight as I can — and flying away! Like this..."
"Careful — you'll fall out."
He heard the sound of a scuffle and Sonya's disapproving voice: "It's past one o'clock."
"Oh, you just ruin everything. Fine — go, go!"
Again all was silent, but Prince Andrew knew she was still sitting there. From time to time he heard a soft rustle, and once a sigh.
"Oh God! Oh God! What does it mean?" she suddenly exclaimed. "Well, off to bed then, if I must!" And she slammed the window shut.

"I might as well not exist for her!" thought Prince Andrew as he listened, for some reason expecting — and fearing — that she might say something about him. "There she is again! As if it were on purpose," he thought.

In his soul there suddenly arose such an unexpected turmoil of youthful thoughts and hopes — so contrary to the whole direction of his life — that, unable to make sense of his own state, he lay down and fell asleep at once.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Next morning, having said goodbye to no one but the count and without waiting for the ladies to appear, Prince Andrew set off for home.

It was already the beginning of June when, on his return journey, he drove into the birch forest where the gnarled old oak had made such a strange and memorable impression on him. In the forest the harness bells sounded even more muffled than they had six weeks before, for now everything was thick, shady, and dense. The young firs scattered through the forest no longer clashed with the general beauty but, blending in with the mood around them, were delicately green with fluffy new shoots.

The whole day had been hot. Somewhere a storm was gathering, but only a small cloud had sprinkled a few raindrops on the road and the juicy leaves. The left side of the forest was dark in shadow; the right side sparkled in the sunlight, wet and glistening and barely stirred by the breeze. Everything was in bloom, the nightingales trilled, and their songs echoed now near, now far away.

"Yes — it was here in this forest, with that oak I agreed with," thought Prince Andrew. "But where is it?" he wondered again, looking to the left side of the road, and without recognizing it, he gazed in admiration at the very oak he had been looking for. The old oak, completely transformed, spread a canopy of rich, dark-green foliage and stood swaying gently, almost trembling, in the rays of the evening sun. Neither gnarled fingers nor old scars nor old doubts and sorrows were anywhere in evidence. Through the tough, century-old bark — even where there were no branches — leaves had sprouted, so fresh and vigorous it was hard to believe the old veteran could have produced them.

"Yes, it is the same oak," thought Prince Andrew, and all at once he was seized by an unreasoning springtime feeling of joy and renewal. All the best moments of his life suddenly rose to his memory. Austerlitz with the vast heavens, his wife's dead, reproachful face, Pierre at the ferry, that girl thrilled by the beauty of the night, and that night itself, and the moon — all of it rushed suddenly into his mind.

"No, life is not over at thirty-one!" Prince Andrew suddenly decided, finally and irrevocably. "It's not enough for me to know what I have inside me — everyone must know it: Pierre, and that young girl who wanted to fly into the sky — everyone must know me, so that my life is not lived for myself alone, apart from everyone else, but so that it is reflected in them all, and they and I may live in harmony!"

On reaching home, Prince Andrew decided to go to Petersburg that autumn and found all sorts of reasons to justify this decision. A whole series of sensible, logical arguments showing that it was essential to go — and even to re-enter the service — kept springing up in his mind. He could not now understand how he had ever doubted the necessity of taking an active part in life, just as a month ago he hadn't understood how the idea of leaving the country could enter his head. It now seemed clear that all his experience of life would be senselessly wasted unless he put it to some use and played an active role again. He didn't even remember how, on the strength of similar flimsy logic, it had previously seemed obvious that he'd be debasing himself if he allowed himself — after the lessons life had taught him — to believe again in the possibility of being useful, and in the possibility of happiness or love. Now reason pointed in exactly the opposite direction. After that trip to Ryazan he found country life dull; his old pursuits no longer interested him, and often, sitting alone in his study, he would get up, go to the mirror, and stare at his own face for a long time. Then he would turn away to look at the portrait of his dead Lise, who, with her hair curled a la grecque, gazed out of the gilt frame tenderly and cheerfully. She no longer spoke those terrible words to him but simply looked at him — merrily, curiously, and questioningly. And Prince Andrew, clasping his hands behind his back, would pace the room for ages, now frowning, now smiling, as he pondered those irrational, inexpressible thoughts — secret as a crime — that altered his entire life and were connected with Pierre, with fame, with the girl at the window, the oak, and woman's beauty and love. And if anyone came into his room at such moments, he was particularly cold, stern, and above all unpleasantly logical.
"My dear," Princess Mary would say, entering at such a moment, "little Nicholas can't go out today — it's very cold."

"If it were hot," Prince Andrew would reply at such times very drily to his sister, "he could go out in his smock. But since it's cold, he must wear warm clothes, which were designed for that purpose. That is the logical consequence of it being cold — not that a child who needs fresh air should be kept indoors." He would add this with exaggerated logic, as if punishing someone for those secret, illogical emotions stirring within him.
At such moments Princess Mary would think how intellectual work dries men up.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Prince Andrew arrived in Petersburg in August 1809. It was the time when the young Speransky was at the peak of his fame and his reforms were being pushed forward with the greatest energy. That same August, the Emperor was thrown from his carriage, injured his leg, and spent three weeks at Peterhof, receiving Speransky every day and no one else. At that time the two famous decrees were being prepared that so agitated society — abolishing court ranks and requiring examinations for the grades of Collegiate Assessor and State Councilor — and not just these, but a whole state constitution intended to transform the existing system of government in Russia: legal, administrative, and financial, from the Council of State down to the district courts. Now those vague liberal dreams with which Emperor Alexander had ascended the throne, and which he had tried to realize with the help of his associates Czartoryski, Novosiltsev, Kochubey, and Strogonov — whom he himself jokingly called his Comite de salut public — were taking concrete shape.

Now all these men had been replaced by Speransky on the civilian side and Arakcheev on the military. Soon after his arrival, Prince Andrew — as a gentleman of the chamber — presented himself at court and at a levee. The Emperor, though he saw him twice, did not favor him with a single word. It had always seemed to Prince Andrew that he was antipathetic to the Emperor, that the sovereign disliked his face and personality — and in the cold, distant glance Alexander gave him, he found further confirmation. The courtiers explained the Emperor's neglect as displeasure at Bolkonski's not having served since 1805.

"I know perfectly well that one can't help one's sympathies and antipathies," thought Prince Andrew, "so there's no point presenting my proposal for army reform to the Emperor personally. The project will speak for itself."

He mentioned what he had written to an old field marshal who was a friend of his father's. The field marshal gave him an appointment, received him graciously, and promised to inform the Emperor. A few days later, Prince Andrew received notice that he was to see the Minister of War, Count Arakcheev.
On the appointed day, Prince Andrew entered Count Arakcheev's waiting room at nine in the morning.
He didn't know Arakcheev personally, had never seen him, and everything he'd heard about the man inspired little respect.

"He is the Minister of War, a man trusted by the Emperor — I needn't concern myself with his personal qualities. He's been asked to review my project, and he alone can get it approved," thought Prince Andrew as he waited among various important and unimportant people in Arakcheev's anteroom.

During his time as an aide-de-camp, Prince Andrew had seen the waiting rooms of many powerful men and knew the different types well. Arakcheev's anteroom had a very distinctive character. The faces of the minor petitioners showed embarrassment and servility; the faces of those of higher rank wore a shared expression of unease, masked by an air of indifference and ironic self-mockery directed at themselves, their situation, and the person they were waiting to see. Some paced thoughtfully; others whispered and laughed. Prince Andrew heard the nickname "Sila Andreevich" and the words "Uncle will give it to us hot" — in reference to Arakcheev. One general, an important person, was clearly offended at having to wait so long and sat crossing and uncrossing his legs, smiling contemptuously to himself.

But the moment the door opened, every face showed one expression only: fear. Prince Andrew asked the duty adjutant a second time to announce him, but received an ironic look and was told his turn would come. After several others had been shown in and out of the minister's office, an officer entered whose humiliated, frightened manner struck Prince Andrew. This man's audience lasted a long time. Then suddenly a harsh, grating voice was heard from behind the door, and the officer — pale-faced and trembling — came out through the waiting room, clutching his head.
After this, Prince Andrew was led to the door, and the duty officer whispered: "To the right, by the window."

Prince Andrew entered a plain, tidy room and saw at the table a man of about forty with a long torso, a long close-cropped head, deep wrinkles, scowling brows above dull greenish-hazel eyes, and a large, overhanging red nose. Arakcheev turned his head toward him without actually looking at him.
"What is your petition?" asked Arakcheev.
"I am not petitioning, your excellency," Prince Andrew replied quietly.
Arakcheev's eyes turned toward him.
"Sit down," he said. "Prince Bolkonski?"
"I'm not petitioning for anything. His Majesty the Emperor has been pleased to send your excellency a project I submitted..."

"You see, my dear sir, I have read your project," Arakcheev interrupted, beginning amiably enough but then — again without looking at Prince Andrew — gradually lapsing into a tone of grumbling contempt. "You are proposing new military laws? There are plenty of laws already, but no one to enforce the old ones. Nowadays everyone designs laws — it's easier to write than to act."
"I came at His Majesty the Emperor's wish to learn how your excellency proposes to deal with the memorandum I submitted," said Prince Andrew politely.

"I have written my comments on your memorandum and forwarded it to the committee. I do not approve of it," said Arakcheev, standing up and taking a paper from his desk. "Here!" And he handed it to Prince Andrew.

Scrawled across the paper in pencil, without capitals, misspelled, and without punctuation, was: "unsoundly constructed because resembles an imitation of the french military code and from the articles of war needlessly deviating."
"To which committee has the memorandum been referred?" asked Prince Andrew.
"To the Committee on Army Regulations. And I have recommended that your honor be appointed a member — but without salary."
Prince Andrew smiled.
"I don't want one."
"A member without salary," repeated Arakcheev. "I have the honor... Well! Call the next one! Who else is there?" he shouted, bowing Prince Andrew out.
